note: One problem per week, each chosen to be doable with what the notes cover by then. `from` is the Monday the week starts; the site shows the latest entry whose date has arrived, so the list can run ahead without revealing anything. Add a row rather than editing the current one, so the history stays readable.

weeks.why: Four ways to initialise one variable, and only one of them is safe by default. Worth settling early, because every line you write from here on picks one.
Your notes have sizeof and alignment fresh. This is the same idea pushed one step further, into why a struct is bigger than the sum of its parts.
The note on why to avoid unsigned integers, made concrete: a comparison that is obviously true and is false.
The first problem where you write and compile real C++. Functions, parameters, std::cin and std::cout, and nothing else.
Shadowing is in your notes and it is the only one of these ideas that bites silently — the program compiles, runs, and uses the wrong variable.
You have header guards written down. This is what one looks like when it is subtly wrong, which is how they always go wrong.
Unscoped enumerations are the newest thing in your notes, and their implicit conversion to int is the part that surprises everyone.
Your data-alignment note, applied to a struct you have to lay out by hand. The first problem here that is about the machine rather than the language.

weeks.note: One else-if chain. Every boundary is a different answer, which is the whole exercise.
Your first loop, with the same ordering trap as last week one level up.
A while loop over std::cin, which is how you read input of unknown length.
Peeling digits with % and /. The loop you will write a hundred times.
One small function, called twice. The point is that the logic appears once.
A whole line with getline, then a char at a time. A char is a small integer.
The first problem whose answer needs all the data at once, which is what a vector is for.
A predicate function plus a loop, and a time limit that insists on the square-root bound.
A function that changes its caller's variable. Drop the & once, deliberately, and watch nothing happen.
Two indices walking inwards, and the unsigned underflow that waits for you there.
const& to read, & to write - three signatures, three different contracts.
++count[word] does the whole job, and a sorted container gives you the output order free.
Write std::find yourself, forwards and backwards. The backward loop is the lesson.
Three counters and an invariant that checks your own work.
The same four bytes read two ways, and the same 32 bits read signed and unsigned.
A first look at Rust: who owns this String, and what the compiler says when you use it twice.
A stack in a fixed array. Count, not top-index, and refuse rather than overwrite.
Binary search written from its invariant, which is the only way it comes out right.
Many readers or one writer, and why that one rule removes a whole class of bug.
FIFO, LRU and optimal on the same reference string, including Belady's anomaly.
